title: Retool alternatives: how to pick the right internal app builder in 2026
summary: Jet Admin, Appsmith, ToolJet, Budibase, UI Bakery, Superblocks, DronaHQ, Refine and Power Apps compared on pricing model, self-hosting and governance.
body_markdown:
Retool is very good at what it does, which is why people rarely leave over features. They leave over the bill as the builder count grows, over self-hosting sitting behind an enterprise contract, or because the people who need to change a tool are not the people who can read its JavaScript.


This guide covers nine credible replacements and says plainly which fits which situation. Pricing was checked in September 2026.


> For governed apps on the data you already run, Jet Admin. For the strongest open-source option overall, Appsmith. For open source with AI built in, ToolJet. For full data sovereignty on a small team, Budibase. For a visual builder that still lets engineers in, UI Bakery. For programmable API-first apps, Superblocks. For mobile alongside desktop, DronaHQ. For owning real React code, Refine. And if the company runs on Microsoft, Power Apps.

## What is Retool, and why look for alternatives?


Retool assembles internal tools from a component library bound to your databases and APIs, with JavaScript wherever the visual layer stops. It is the most refined product in this category, it serves over 500,000 users, and companies including Amazon, Stripe, Netflix, Plaid, DoorDash and Coinbase run internal systems on it. Teams leave for four reasons.


### The price steps rather than slopes


At small scale Retool is not expensive: roughly $10 per builder and $5 per internal user monthly. The problem is the shape of the curve. Add builders and it climbs; need governance features and you land on the Business tier at around $50 per builder, which is a step rather than a slope. Platforms that decouple price from headcount flatten out exactly where Retool accelerates.


### Self-hosting sits behind an enterprise contract


This is the one that stings for teams who came to Retool from an open-source tool. Running it inside your own network is an enterprise-plan feature, so the answer to a security review is a sales call. Appsmith, ToolJet and Budibase give you the same answer for free.


### Only developers can maintain what gets built


Retool assumes JavaScript. That is fine while the engineer who built the tool is still on the team and a problem the moment the tool belongs to operations and the engineer has moved on. The question is not which platform is easier today, but who edits this in a year.


### AI arrived as an add-on rather than as the product


Superblocks, UI Bakery, ToolJet and Jet Admin generate apps from a description as part of the platform. Retool has its own AI and Agents, billed separately. For one tool the difference is a afternoon; across a backlog it decides whether the backlog moves.


### When Retool is still the right choice


If your builders are engineers, your tools stay internal, cloud hosting is acceptable and the component polish matters to you, Retool remains the strongest product here. Switching would cost weeks and buy nothing.


## Types of Retool alternatives


The alternatives to Retool fall into five categories, and picking the category first removes most of the list.


- Open-source, self-hosting first. No licence, no seat cap, your infrastructure. Appsmith, ToolJet, Budibase.
- Commercial platforms for mixed teams. Governance and generation included rather than tiered. Jet Admin, UI Bakery.
- Programmable app engines. Closer to a framework than a builder. Superblocks, DronaHQ.
- Code-ownership frameworks. You get React, not a canvas. Refine.
- Ecosystem-bundled options. Microsoft Power Apps.


## What to look for


Five things decide most of these evaluations. The pricing unit, because per-builder, per-end-user and flat models diverge sharply once a tool becomes popular. Whether self-hosting exists at all and on which tier, since that single answer removes half the list. Who can maintain the result, which is a different question from who can build it. Data access, meaning the databases, warehouses and APIs you actually run rather than a copy. And governance depth: row-level rules, audit logs, SSO and separate environments, and which plan they appear on.


## 1. Jet Admin, best for governed apps on the data you already run


**Pros and cons.** Generates the tool from a description on your existing data, with permissions and deployment options included rather than tiered. It is commercial and not open-source, so teams that require modifiable source should look at Appsmith, ToolJet or Budibase below, and it is not intended for marketing sites or consumer products.


**Key features.** Connects your own databases, warehouses and APIs with blending across sources. Granular component access and values passed between pages, server-side dynamic filtering for multi-tenancy, approval flows and conditionals without code, with JavaScript to extend. Figma import. Row and field level permissions, SSO, and self-hosted or on-premise deployment on the same product rather than on a separate contract.


**Pricing.** Free plan with 20+ integrations and Figma import. Internal tools from $30 per user, with client portals priced separately from internal seats.


**Best for** mixed teams where operations people need to change tools without filing an engineering ticket, and where IT has to sign off on where the data lives.


## 2. Appsmith, best open-source alternative overall


**Pros and cons.** The most complete free option: self-host everything with no seat cost and full functionality. In exchange you run the infrastructure, and the builder assumes developers.


**Key features.** Open-source low-code platform with a 64-column canvas that gives finer placement control than Retool’s 12-column grid, JavaScript throughout, and broad database and API connectivity.


**Pricing.** Free when self-hosted, for unlimited users. Paid cloud tiers available.


**Best for** engineering teams who want the source, no per-seat cost, and control over deployment.


## 3. ToolJet, best open source with AI generation


**Pros and cons.** Matches Appsmith on the open-source guarantees and adds application generation from a description. Some advanced capabilities sit behind the premium tier.


**Key features.** 80+ data source integrations and 82+ pre-built components, with tables, kanban boards, charts, calendars, file uploads and a QR scanner on the canvas. JavaScript, Python or SQL queries directly against a source. Self-hosting on Docker or Kubernetes; enterprise adds SSO, Git and audit logs. Plugin marketplace.


**Pricing.** Free self-hosted, with paid cloud and enterprise tiers.


**Best for** teams that want open source without giving up AI-assisted building.


## 4. Budibase, best for full data sovereignty on a small team


**Pros and cons.** Generates CRUD interfaces from a data source in seconds and is free to self-host with unlimited apps, automations and users. UI polish is limited once applications get complex.


**Key features.** Hybrid data model: create tables inside the platform or connect PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, MongoDB, CouchDB, Supabase, Firebase, Google Sheets and Airtable. Strong form and workflow automation for approvals, onboarding and compliance requests. Publishes public apps and portals, which most internal tool builders will not do.


**Pricing.** Free on the open-source tier. Paid plans around $50 per month for creators plus $5 per end user.


**Reviews.** G2 4.5 out of 5.


**Best for** small teams building CRUD tools and approval workflows with no licence budget.


## 5. UI Bakery, best for mixed teams that still want custom code


**Pros and cons.** A visual builder with a genuine escape hatch into code, and per-developer pricing that is materially below Retool’s at the same headcount. Not open-source, and the community is smaller.


**Key features.** Drag-and-drop canvas covering tables, lists, cards, forms, multi-step workflows, charts and file uploads, with responsive layouts generated for desktop, tablet and mobile. Connects REST, GraphQL, OpenAPI and webhooks plus the usual databases. RBAC, separate development, staging and production environments, audit logs, Git on paid plans, cloud or self-hosted. AI app generation.


**Pricing.** Around $20 per developer per month, which works out near $60 for three developers.


**Best for** teams who want more pre-built components and tighter layout control than Retool without a developer-only platform.


## 6. Superblocks, best for programmable, API-first internal apps


**Pros and cons.** Closer to an app engine than a builder, with hybrid deployment that keeps sensitive data inside your network. Steeper learning curve for non-technical users.


**Key features.** An app builder, an API builder and a workflow engine in one product. JavaScript and Python for custom logic, 50+ integrations, 100+ UI components, background workflows with cron and triggers, and an open-source on-premise agent. Raised $23 million in Series A funding in 2025.


**Pricing.** Around $100 for up to 15 builders billed annually, which is where it separates from per-seat models.


**Best for** engineering teams transforming data across many services who want price decoupled from headcount.


## 7. DronaHQ, best for mobile alongside internal tools


**Pros and cons.** Treats mobile as a first-class target rather than an afterthought, and prices with unlimited end users. Smaller community and fewer templates than the leaders.


**Key features.** Internal tools, mobile apps, Android apps and progressive web apps from one builder, with custom components in HTML and JavaScript. Workflow engine covering approvals, cron jobs, data-change triggers and notifications by email, SMS or Slack. RBAC, three environments, audit logs and Git integration.


**Pricing.** Around $100 for the Starter plan with unlimited users.


**Best for** teams that need field or mobile apps alongside desktop internal tools.


## 8. Refine, best for engineering teams that want real code


**Pros and cons.** Not a builder at all: an open-source React framework for internal tools. You get a codebase you own outright, and you give up the thing that lets a non-developer change a screen.


**Key features.** React and TypeScript framework with data providers for common backends, auth, routing and access control as first-class concerns, and no vendor runtime.


**Pricing.** Open-source and free; you provide the hosting.


**Best for** teams whose objection to Retool is lock-in rather than price.


## 9. Microsoft Power Apps, best inside the Microsoft stack


**Pros and cons.** Strong when the data already sits in Microsoft’s cloud and the licences are already paid. Against that: a formula language that limits deeper customisation, licensing complexity, and less flexible UI.


**Key features.** Form-based app builder integrated with Microsoft 365, Power Platform and Dataverse, suited to data collection and workflows over SharePoint, Excel and Dynamics.


**Pricing.** Per user or per app within the Microsoft ecosystem.


**Best for** business units building operational apps inside the suite they already pay for.


## Also worth knowing


Forest Admin generates an admin panel straight from your database schema, which suits teams whose whole requirement is back-office CRUD. Lowcoder is a direct open-source alternative that surfaces on this search often. Gumloop targets non-technical teams building tools without SQL, free then around $37 a month. And on the heavyweight end, OutSystems, Appian and ServiceNow App Engine are enterprise process platforms rather than internal tool builders, appropriate only when process automation across the business is the actual requirement.


## The question that settles it


Two of these categories look interchangeable and are not. If your objection to Retool is the bill, the answer is a platform that prices by something other than headcount, and Appsmith, ToolJet, Budibase, Superblocks and DronaHQ all qualify. If your objection is that only engineers can maintain what gets built, price is beside the point and you want generation and a visual layer non-developers can use.


Teams that answer the second question with an open-source tool tend to be back on this page a year later, having swapped a licence cost for an engineering cost. Decide which one you are actually solving before comparing tiers.


## Choosing the best Retool alternative for your team type


The best retool alternatives are context-dependent. Here's how to translate the earlier comparisons into concrete recommendations by team profile:


- **Small, non-technical operations teams** needing simple internal tools fast: lean toward no code platforms like Glide, Softr, or a higher-level builder like Jet Admin that can generate interfaces quickly. No-code platforms require no programming skills to use, which keeps adoption fast.
- **Mid-sized SaaS or startup teams** with a few engineers owning internal apps: consider Jet Admin, Appsmith, or ToolJet depending on your appetite for self-hosting vs. managed cloud and how much custom code you want to write. A free plan or free tier lets you validate before committing.
- **Large enterprises** with strong IT and security functions: shortlist Superblocks, Power Apps, Jet Admin, and possibly open-source platforms with self-hosting, depending on regulatory requirements and Microsoft adoption. Enterprise pricing and enterprise plans should include SSO, audit logs, and on premise deployment.
- **Agencies or B2B companies shipping client portals:** focus on Jet Admin, Softr, Bubble, or similar tools with stronger client-facing UI capabilities and robust authentication for external users.
- **Teams prioritizing AI-native workflows:** consider platforms emphasizing natural language prompts and AI generation, while checking governance maturity. An ai app builder can dramatically cut time to first version, but production apps still benefit from developer oversight.


Weight data security, governance, and app criticality more heavily when internal tools touch PII, finance, healthcare, or regulated workloads. The upcoming migration and governance sections can be turned into an internal decision document.


## Migration checklist: moving from Retool to an alternative


Switching internal-tool platforms is less about code and more about planning: inventorying apps, data sources, and stakeholders.


- **Inventory and categorize existing Retool apps.** Group by criticality (mission-critical vs. convenience), by department (ops, support, finance), and by complexity (CRUD-only vs. heavy custom logic and JS). Identify which are unlimited apps and which have per end user pricing implications.
- **Map data sources and auth patterns.** Document which databases, APIs, and third-party SaaS tools each app touches. Record user groups, roles, SSO setups, and any row-level security rules.
- **Choose target platforms per app type.** Simple CRUD dashboards might move to Jet Admin or Budibase. Complex React-like frontends might migrate to Superblocks or custom code backed by Xano. Admin panels with workflow automation could go to ToolJet or Appsmith.
- **Run one to two pilot migrations.** Pick medium-complexity apps, rebuild them in the target platform, and validate performance, usability, and security with real internal users. Use this to benchmark build speed and data connectivity.
- **Plan coexistence and cutover.** Operate Retool and the new platform side-by-side for a defined window. Ensure links, bookmarks, and permissions are updated. Communicate timelines to stakeholders clearly.
- **Decommission and archive.** Once traffic has shifted, archive Retool apps, revoke credentials, and ensure data retention and compliance obligations are met.


AI-enabled builders, including Jet Admin, can reduce rebuild time by generating UIs and logic from existing schemas or plain language app descriptions. Create internal runbooks for each migration phase.


## Governance, data security, and compliance considerations


For many organizations, especially in finance, healthcare, or B2B SaaS, governance and data security matter more than the visual builder experience when choosing a retool alternative.


**Key governance dimensions to review with each vendor:**


- **Authentication and authorization.** Single sign on via SAML, OAuth, SCIM provisioning, just-in-time provisioning, granular roles, and row-level security where needed. Role based access control should extend to external users and internal users alike.
- **Data residency and deployment.** Cloud regions, VPC peering, private cloud or self-hosted options, air-gapped deployments, and how data traverses between the app builder and your data sources. On premise deployment matters for regulated industries.
- **Auditability.** Detailed audit logs of user actions, changes to apps, and production incidents. Integration with SIEM tools where available. Version control through git sync supports change tracking.
- **Change management.** Staging environments, approvals, Git integration, CI/CD, and the ability to roll back deployments safely.


Open-source platforms shift some security responsibility onto internal teams. While they can be deployed in tightly controlled environments, patching, hardening, and monitoring become in-house tasks.


Jet Admin invests in enterprise-grade security and governance, including SSO, audit logs, granular access controls, and deployment options suited for data-sensitive environments. Verify exact certifications, controls, and deployment models directly from the[current Jet Admin documentation](https://www.jetadmin.io/features) before making commitments.


Security, DevOps, and data teams should participate early in any Retool replacement project. Proof-of-concept deployments should include security reviews, not just feature demos.


## Conclusion: narrowing down your list of Retool alternatives


There is no single "best Retool alternative." Instead, there are clusters of tools optimized for internal tools, open-source control, Microsoft ecosystems, client portals, or AI-native workflows. The right choice depends on your team's skills, deployment requirements, and whether you're building custom internal tools, client portals, or mobile apps.


Use the 8-part evaluation framework, build speed, data connectivity, extensibility, auth and permissions, deployment, governance, pricing model, and maintenance, and turn it into a concrete comparison sheet across your top three to five candidates.


**Example shortlists for common situations:**


- "We're a scale-up with 5–10 engineers and many internal users" → evaluate Jet Admin, Retool, Appsmith, and ToolJet.
- "We're an enterprise with Microsoft 365 everywhere" → compare Power Apps, Jet Admin, Superblocks, and possibly open-source if self-hosting is mandatory.
- "We need polished client portals on top of existing data" → look at Jet Admin, Softr, Bubble.


If you're ready to test your shortlist, consider trialing[Jet Admin](https://www.jetadmin.io/) alongside at least one other contender. Benchmark build speed, data connectivity, and governance in your own environment with your real data sources. That's the only way to know which platform actually fits.


## FAQ about Retool alternatives


These FAQs cover questions not fully explored in the main sections.


### What is the best Retool alternative for non-technical teams?


Non-technical or lightly technical teams usually prefer true no code tools such as Glide, Softr, or a higher-level app builder like Jet Admin, which can generate much of the UI and custom logic from existing data and simple configuration instead of JavaScript. These platforms let non technical users ship working web apps and internal tools without writing code.


### Can I replace Retool with open-source tools without increasing risk?


Open-source platforms like Appsmith, ToolJet, and Budibase can absolutely replace Retool in many scenarios. However, risk shifts from vendor to internal teams, they must handle hosting, backups, security patches, and monitoring. Appsmith offers a free self-hosted edition with no user limits, which keeps license costs at zero, but operational overhead is real. For some organizations this trade-off is acceptable; for others a managed no code platform with strong SLAs is safer.


### How important is native mobile support when choosing a Retool alternative?


Importance depends on where users work. If most usage is desktop-based (ops, finance, back-office), browser-first tools like Retool or Jet Admin are often enough. If teams are in the field or on the go, platforms like Glide, Power Apps, or others with native mobile apps and native mobile app support can materially improve adoption.


### Do AI-native builders fully remove the need for developers?


AI-native builders and assistants can dramatically cut time-to-first-version by generating internal apps and workflows from natural language prompts. But production-grade tools still benefit from developer oversight for security, data modeling, performance, and integration edge cases. Treat AI generation as a starting point, not the finish line.


### How long does it typically take to migrate off Retool?


Timelines vary by app count and complexity. Small teams replacing a handful of dashboards may migrate in weeks, while large enterprises with dozens of mission-critical internal tools should plan for a phased migration over several months, including pilots, coexistence with the team plan on both platforms, and formal cutover windows.
